records.name: Nayarit
records.summary:
Nayarit was the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfeminicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in early 2024 — a step the capital followed in July 2024 with its 70-year 'Paola Buenrostro law', named for a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose attacker was released after 48 hours despite footage and witnesses and has not been caught since. Nayarit's law also lets friends, not only relatives, claim bodies and drive investigations, which matters where families disown trans relatives.

That statute landed against more than 95% impunity for homicides in Mexico in 2022, believed higher for transfeminicides, so it records official posture more than proven protection. No other Nayarit-specific incidents or enforcement records are supported by the vetted sources; the national picture otherwise governs — by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six enacting none.

records.name: Queretaro de Arteaga
records.summary: A split record: Querétaro's congress banned conversion practices on 29 June 2023 with penalties of 2-6 years, yet it is one of six states Human Rights Watch (March 2025) lists as having never legislated any legal-gender-recognition procedure, leaving trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched. No state-specific incident or enforcement evidence was identified.

records.name: San Luis Potosi
records.summary: No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found; the state's place in the national map is ordinary compliance: a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure, with implementing regulations set by gubernatorial decree.

records.name: Sinaloa
records.summary:
No Sinaloa-specific statutes or provisions are supported by the vetted sources for this map. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.

Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, Sinaloa's own legal record on this map is thin: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections; general-security caution in the region applies independently of any local rights framework.

records.name: Sonora
records.summary:
No Sonora-specific laws, incidents or enforcement patterns are supported by the vetted sources for this map, and the claim that it sits outside the documented problem categories cannot itself be verified from them. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.

Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, Sonora's own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility.

records.name: Tabasco
records.summary:
Tabasco has enacted no legal procedure for recognising gender identity. A Human Rights Watch report co-produced with a local inclusion centre (March 2024) documented that the absence of any recognition procedure leaves trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched and exposed to police and institutional mistreatment.

By March 2025, Human Rights Watch counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender recognition and named six — among them Tabasco, the subject of the dedicated 2024 report — whose legislatures had enacted none. For a visible trans visitor the document mismatch is the practical trigger: an ID that does not match presentation invites the questioning and mistreatment the report records.

records.name: Tamaulipas
records.summary:
Tamaulipas is among the six Mexican states whose legislatures have enacted no legal procedure for recognising gender identity, per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count of 22 of 32 states having legislated one. Where no procedure exists, trans residents' identity documents remain permanently mismatched with any official record of who they are.

The consequences of that absence are documented in the companion 2024 Human Rights Watch report on one such state: mismatched documents invite exactly the police checks and institutional mistreatment that most endanger a visible trans visitor in daily interactions.

records.name: Tlaxcala
records.summary:
Tlaxcala is not among the six Mexican states whose legislatures have enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure, per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count (22 of 32 states have legislated one).

No Tlaxcala-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern targeting transgender people appears in the surviving sources; Mexico's national criminal law and gender-recognition regime apply here as elsewhere in the country.
